implementation_notes: Drogon is the mainstream C++ framework that ships sessions: HttpAppFramework::instance().enableSession(timeout, sameSite) turns them on (1200 s default, 0 keeps the record for the application's whole lifetime) and every request then carries a drogon::Session through req->session(), a thread-safe, typed key/value bag with insert/get/modify/find that the framework keeps on the server while only the SessionID cookie travels to the browser. That replaces the classic role structure - identifier generation, registry lookup, cookie binding - with one framework call, and the session object is available in handlers and filters alike (the documented usage pattern is a filter that rate-limits by session). The remaining decision is deployment: with the in-process store a conversation is pinned to one instance, so a farm needs a shared store or sticky routing, which the framework does not decide for you.
pitfalls: Session support is off by default; enabling it also means clients without cookie support create a new record for every request, which the documentation calls out as wasted memory and compute.
The framework store is per process: an in-process session pins the conversation to one instance unless a shared store or sticky routing is added.
enableSession(0) means 'never expire', which is rarely what a production deployment wants; the timeout must be chosen deliberately.

variants.name: Boost.Beast server + hand-written session table
variants.idiom_name: std::unordered_map<std::string, Session> behind std::mutex, swept on a timer
variants.implementation_notes: When Beast/Asio is already the HTTP layer and no session-aware framework is in the stack, the classic structure is written by hand: the handler parses the Cookie header, the table maps identifier -> session object under a std::mutex (or one shard per worker thread), and a periodic task drops idle records. Boost.Beast provides HTTP messages and connections, not a session abstraction, so identifier generation, expiry and serialization policy remain application code - this variant is justified for a small, fixed set of values and a single-instance deployment, but it reimplements what a session framework would otherwise own.
pitfalls: Every thread running the io_context shares the table: unlock the mutex around user code and the race is back; hold it and blocking handlers serialize the server.
Without a sweeper the map grows without bound; and because it is process memory, a second worker or a restart silently empties every conversation.
The Cookie header is attacker-controlled text: parse it strictly (length, charset, one value per name) and never hash or index on it unchecked.

variants.name: Session record in Redis (hiredis), shared across instances
variants.idiom_name: Redis hash/string per session id with TTL (hiredis client)
variants.implementation_notes: The deployment variant that removes affinity: keep the payload in Redis under a key derived from the session identifier, set with an expiry so the store itself forgets idle conversations, and let every instance read and write the same record; hiredis is the usual C client for that. The carrier and rotation policy do not change - only the owner of the payload - but resolving a request now depends on the network, so timeouts, pooling and a stated failure mode (fail closed for authenticated routes) become part of the realization, and concurrent writers need a version or last-write-wins rule.
pitfalls: A store outage is now a session outage: every request fails to resolve its conversation, so the error path must be explicit (fail closed for privileged routes, never silently anonymous).
Read-modify-write across instances races: two concurrent requests from one client can interleave GET/SET and lose an update unless the record carries a version or the conversation is single-writer.
Redis replies must be freed (redisReply) and connections pooled/shared correctly across threads; the naive 'connect per request' version both leaks and collapses under load.
